analysis.evidence: אֶת־זַרְעֲךָ marks “your offspring” as the object, and כַּעֲפַר הָאָרֶץ supplies the comparison, “like the dust of the earth.” The following clause explains the likeness in terms of how many descendants there will be.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וְ precedes a Qal perfect with the first-person common singular ending ־תִּי. The weqatal form continues the promise with future force.
Hebrew direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: God promises Abram, “I will make your descendants like the dust of the earth.” The comparison turns on counting the grains of dust and expresses how numerous Abram’s descendants will be.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular common noun in the construct state with a second-person masculine singular possessive suffix referring to Abram. The noun is collective.

analysis.evidence: Abram’s descendants are compared to the dust of the earth. The following clause repeats עֲפַר הָאָרֶץ as the object of לִמְנוֹת, “to count,” making the number of dust particles the point of the comparison.
analysis.morphology: The comparative preposition כַּ means “like.” The masculine singular noun עֲפַר is in construct with הָאָרֶץ, “the earth.”

analysis.evidence: כַּעֲפַר הָאָרֶץ means “like the dust of the ground.” The comparison draws on the countless particles of dust on the ground to describe the number of Abram’s descendants.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הָ־ precedes a common noun of both genders in the singular absolute. The noun completes the construct phrase כַּעֲפַר הָאָרֶץ.

analysis.evidence: אֲשֶׁר introduces the consequence of the comparison with the dust of the earth. אִם introduces the condition “if anyone can count the dust of the earth,” and גַּם זַרְעֲךָ יִמָּנֶה gives its consequence, “your offspring too can be counted.”
analysis.morphology: An uninflected relative particle used as a conjunction, with no prefix or suffix.
